text: About 5,000 years ago, the ancestors of the Māori lived in Taiwan, and their descendants moved from island to island across Polynesia.
On the way they left behind a kind of pottery called Lapita pottery.
src: their ancestry, as part of the wider Austronesian peoples, goes back about 5,000 years to the Indigenous peoples of Taiwan, whose descendants moved through the Philippines, along the edge of Melanesia / and across Polynesia to New Zealand last of all
along the edge of Melanesia, where they left Lapita pottery

text: About 700 years ago, they sailed in great canoes called waka and settled New Zealand, last of all the Polynesian lands.
Māori also call themselves tangata whenua, “people of the land”.
src: The ancestors of the Māori sailed from eastern Polynesia in ocean-going waka and settled New Zealand around 1250–1350, last of all the Polynesian lands / the main settlement came in the first half of the 14th century
also call themselves tangata whenua, “people of the land”

text: They found forests full of birds, such as the moa, which could weigh as much as 250 kilograms.
Most early villages were near the coast, and Otago was the centre of their culture.
src: The settlers found a forested land full of birds, among them several species of moa weighing from 20 to 250 kg
most villages lay on or near the coast, the Otago region was the centre of cultural development

text: Carvers made fine canoes and great meeting houses, and ornaments of pounamu, or greenstone.
Poi, balls of dried flax on strings, are swung and tapped to make rhythms.
src: The Classic period is marked by finely made pounamu (greenstone) weapons and ornaments, by elaborately carved canoes, a tradition later extended to the great carved meeting houses
rhythmic ones such as poi, balls of dried flax on strings that are swung and tapped

text: Europeans arrived about 250 years ago, and new guns and diseases brought war and death.
About 185 years ago chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi with Britain, but later Māori lost most of their land.
src: 1769: James Cook’s first voyage brings the first lasting contact between Māori and Europeans / The new muskets set off the Musket Wars between iwi / Epidemics of influenza, measles and smallpox killed between 10 and 50 per cent of Māori
6 February 1840: The Treaty of Waitangi is first signed at Waitangi by the British Crown and Māori chiefs / suffered war, disease and the loss of most of their land

text: Today Māori lead a strong revival of their language, te reo Māori, which is an official language.
Family, the whānau, and the old ties of kinship remain at the heart of Māori life.
src: today they lead a strong revival of their language and culture / te reo Māori is an official language
The marae, the whānau and the old ties of kinship remain central to Māori life.
